claims.evidence: This is supported by established evolutionary biology knowledge.

claims.claim: Placental mammals are characterized by a long gestation with a high maternal investment during pregnancy.
claims.source: Placental mammals are characterized by a long gestation with a high maternal investment during pregnancy, and a considerable degree of both orofacial and neurocranial development occurring in the embryo in utero.
claims.evidence: This is supported by established knowledge about placental mammal reproduction.

claims.claim: A considerable degree of both orofacial and neurocranial development occurs in the placental embryo in utero.
claims.source: Placental mammals are characterized by a long gestation with a high maternal investment during pregnancy, and a considerable degree of both orofacial and neurocranial development occurring in the embryo in utero.
claims.evidence: This is supported by established knowledge about placental mammal development.

claims.claim: Placental young experience little functional constraint during early developmental stages.
claims.source: As a result, placental young experience little functional constraint during early developmental stages.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the protected in utero environment of placental mammals.

claims.claim: Marsupials have a short gestation and give birth to highly altricial young that must crawl to the teat.
claims.source: By contrast, marsupials have a short gestation and give birth to highly altricial young that must crawl to the teat, typically located within the maternal pouch, where they complete the remainder of their development ex utero.
claims.evidence: This is supported by established knowledge about marsupial reproduction.

claims.claim: Marsupials complete the remainder of their development ex utero in the maternal pouch.
claims.source: By contrast, marsupials have a short gestation and give birth to highly altricial young that must crawl to the teat, typically located within the maternal pouch, where they complete the remainder of their development ex utero.
claims.evidence: This is supported by established knowledge about marsupial development.

claims.claim: The unique reproductive method of marsupials is thought to have imposed strong pressures on the evolution and development of the limbs and head.
claims.source: This unique reproductive method is thought to have imposed strong pressures on the evolution and development of the limbs and head.
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research on marsupial development.

claims.claim: Marsupials show accelerated development of the nasal cavity, tongue, oral bones, and musculature relative to the development of the posterior end of the body.
claims.source: In particular, marsupials show accelerated development of the nasal cavity, tongue, oral bones, and musculature relative to the development of the posterior end of the body (Nunn and Smith, 1998; Smith, 2006; Smith, 2001a; Cook et al., 2021), and generally when compared to placental embryonic development (Nunn and Smith, 1998; Smith, 2006; Smith, 1997).
claims.evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous research.

claims.claim: Marsupials show accelerated development of orofacial structures when compared to placental embryonic development.
claims.source: In particular, marsupials show accelerated development of the nasal cavity, tongue, oral bones, and musculature relative to the development of the posterior end of the body (Nunn and Smith, 1998; Smith, 2006; Smith, 2001a; Cook et al., 2021), and generally when compared to placental embryonic development (Nunn and Smith, 1998; Smith, 2006; Smith, 1997).
claims.evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous research.

claims.claim: Aspects of the peripheral nervous system appear to be accelerated in the marsupial face.
claims.source: Additionally, aspects of the peripheral nervous system appear to be accelerated in the face.
claims.evidence: This is supported by observations described in the manuscript and citations to previous research.

claims.claim: Large medial nasal swellings are observed early in marsupial development that are innervated and proposed to be necessary for the sensory needs of newborn young in their journey to the pouch.
claims.source: We and others have observed large medial nasal swellings early in marsupial development that are innervated and proposed to be necessary for the sensory needs of newborn young in their journey to the pouch (Veitch et al., 2000; Jones and Munger, 1985; Waite et al., 1994).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research including observations by the authors.

claims.claim: Comparative morphometric studies have provided evidence that the difference in craniofacial development has imposed different regimes of constraint on marsupial and placental mammals.
claims.source: Comparative morphometric studies have provided a wealth of evidence that this stark difference in craniofacial development has imposed different regimes of constraint on marsupial and placental mammals (Nunn and Smith, 1998; Smith, 2006; Cook et al., 2021; Smith, 1997; Spiekman and Werneburg, 2017; Koyabu et al., 2014; Goswami et al., 2016) with marsupials in particular showing significantly less interspecies variation in orofacial structures and nasal morphology than placental mammals (Goswami et al., 2016; Sears, 2004; Hüppi et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous morphometric studies.

claims.claim: Marsupials show significantly less interspecies variation in orofacial structures and nasal morphology than placental mammals.
claims.source: Comparative morphometric studies have provided a wealth of evidence that this stark difference in craniofacial development has imposed different regimes of constraint on marsupial and placental mammals (Nunn and Smith, 1998; Smith, 2006; Cook et al., 2021; Smith, 1997; Spiekman and Werneburg, 2017; Koyabu et al., 2014; Goswami et al., 2016) with marsupials in particular showing significantly less interspecies variation in orofacial structures and nasal morphology than placental mammals (Goswami et al., 2016; Sears, 2004; Hüppi et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claims.claim: The molecular mechanisms that underlie differences in early craniofacial development between marsupial and placental mammals remain poorly understood.
claims.source: In spite of these observations, the molecular mechanisms that underlie these differences in early craniofacial development between marsupial and placental mammals remain poorly understood.
claims.evidence: This is an assessment of the current state of knowledge in the field.

claims.claim: Cis-acting regulatory regions have been proposed to play a significant role in morphological divergence in the face.
claims.source: Cis-acting regulatory regions have been proposed to play a significant role in morphological divergence in the face, with a number of well-described enhancers that fine-tune face shape in mammals (Attanasio et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to Attanasio et al., 2013.

claims.claim: There is evidence of a role for regulatory regions in craniofacial heterochrony in marsupials.
claims.source: There is also some evidence of a role for regulatory regions in craniofacial heterochrony in marsupials.
claims.evidence: This is supported by the subsequent description of a marsupial-specific Sox9 enhancer region.

claims.claim: A marsupial-specific region within a Sox9 enhancer drives early and broad expression in pre-migratory neural crest cell domains contributing to early migration of cranial neural crest cells relative to the mouse.
claims.source: One recent study found a marsupial-specific region within a Sox9 enhancer that drives early and broad expression in pre-migratory neural crest cell domains contributing to early migration of cranial neural crest cells relative to the mouse (Wakamatsu and Suzuki, 2019; Wakamatsu et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to Wakamatsu and Suzuki, 2019 and Wakamatsu et al., 2014.

claims.claim: No study has thus far attempted to compare the overall regulatory landscape between marsupials and placentals at developmentally comparable stages.
claims.source: However, no study has thus far attempted to compare the overall regulatory landscape between marsupials and placentals at developmentally comparable stages.
claims.evidence: This is an assessment of the current state of the literature.

claims.claim: The fat-tailed dunnart has emerged as a tractable marsupial model species.
claims.source: In recent years, the fat-tailed dunnart (Sminthopsis crassicaudata, hereafter referred to as the dunnart) has emerged as a tractable marsupial model species (Cook et al., 2021; Suárez et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to Cook et al., 2021 and Suárez et al., 2017.

claims.claim: Dunnarts are born after 13.5 days of gestation.
claims.source: Dunnarts are born after 13.5 days of gestation and craniofacial heterochrony in line with what has been reported in other marsupials is readily observable (Nunn and Smith, 1998; Smith, 2006; Cook et al., 2021; Smith, 1997; Spiekman and Werneburg, 2017; Koyabu et al., 2014; Goswami et al., 2016), making this species an excellent system for comparative studies with placental models.
claims.evidence: This is a factual statement about dunnart gestation supported by established knowledge.

claims.claim: Craniofacial heterochrony in line with what has been reported in other marsupials is readily observable in dunnarts.
claims.source: Dunnarts are born after 13.5 days of gestation and craniofacial heterochrony in line with what has been reported in other marsupials is readily observable (Nunn and Smith, 1998; Smith, 2006; Cook et al., 2021; Smith, 1997; Spiekman and Werneburg, 2017; Koyabu et al., 2014; Goswami et al., 2016), making this species an excellent system for comparative studies with placental models.
claims.evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous research.

claims.claim: Dunnarts rely entirely on the advanced chondrocranium with bony elements of the skeleton not present until approximately 24 hr after birth.
claims.source: The dunnart provides an ideal model in which to study the regulatory landscape during craniofacial development in marsupials, as they rely entirely on the advanced chondrocranium with bony elements of the skeleton not present until approximately 24 hr after birth (Cook et al., 2021).
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to Cook et al., 2021.

claims.claim: 80,989 regions reproducibly enriched for H3K4me3 were identified in dunnart facial prominence tissue.
claims.source: Peak calling with MACS2 (q < 0.05) identified 80,989 regions reproducibly enriched for H3K4me3 and 121,281 regions reproducibly enriched for H3K27ac in dunnart facial prominence tissue.
claims.evidence: This is supported by the ChIP-seq data analysis described in the Methods and Results.

claims.claim: 121,281 regions reproducibly enriched for H3K27ac were identified in dunnart facial prominence tissue.
claims.source: Peak calling with MACS2 (q < 0.05) identified 80,989 regions reproducibly enriched for H3K4me3 and 121,281 regions reproducibly enriched for H3K27ac in dunnart facial prominence tissue.
claims.evidence: This is supported by the ChIP-seq data analysis described in the Methods and Results.

claims.claim: H3K4me3 often (62% of all H3K4me3 peaks) co-occupied the genome with H3K27ac.
claims.source: Similar to previous studies (Villar et al., 2015; Heintzman et al., 2009; Zhu et al., 2013; Cain et al., 2011; Santos-Rosa et al., 2002), we found that H3K4me3 often (62% of all H3K4me3 peaks) co-occupied the genome with H3K27ac (Figure 1A) while 50% of H3K27ac-enriched regions were only associated with this mark (Figure 1A).
claims.evidence: This is supported by the data presented in Figure 1A and citations to previous studies.

claims.claim: 50% of H3K27ac-enriched regions were only associated with this mark.
claims.source: Similar to previous studies (Villar et al., 2015; Heintzman et al., 2009; Zhu et al., 2013; Cain et al., 2011; Santos-Rosa et al., 2002), we found that H3K4me3 often (62% of all H3K4me3 peaks) co-occupied the genome with H3K27ac (Figure 1A) while 50% of H3K27ac-enriched regions were only associated with this mark (Figure 1A).
claims.evidence: This is supported by the data presented in Figure 1A.

claims.claim: Active enhancers are generally enriched for H3K27ac.
claims.source: Active enhancers are generally enriched for H3K27ac (Villar et al., 2015; Creyghton et al., 2010) while sites of transcription initiation (active promoters) can be identified as being marked by both H3K27ac and H3K4me3 (Cain et al., 2011; Santos-Rosa et al., 2002).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to Villar et al., 2015 and Creyghton et al., 2010.

claims.claim: Sites of transcription initiation (active promoters) can be identified as being marked by both H3K27ac and H3K4me3.
claims.source: Active enhancers are generally enriched for H3K27ac (Villar et al., 2015; Creyghton et al., 2010) while sites of transcription initiation (active promoters) can be identified as being marked by both H3K27ac and H3K4me3 (Cain et al., 2011; Santos-Rosa et al., 2002).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to Cain et al., 2011 and Santos-Rosa et al., 2002.

claims.claim: 66,802 promoters and 60,626 enhancers were initially defined in the dunnart.
claims.source: We initially defined promoters as those marked by only H3K4me3 or with >50% of reciprocal peak length for H3K27ac and H3K4me3 peaks, and enhancers as those marked only by H3K27ac, identifying 66,802 promoters and 60,626 enhancers.
claims.evidence: This is supported by the ChIP-seq data analysis described in the Results.

claims.claim: Enhancers were located on average 77 kb from TSS.
claims.source: Enhancers were located on average 77 kb from TSS, while promoters were located on average 106 kb from the nearest TSS, despite there being a greater number of peaks located <1 kb from the TSS (1008 enhancers vs. 9023 promoters; Figure 1B).
claims.evidence: This is supported by the data presented in Figure 1B.

claims.claim: Promoters were located on average 106 kb from the nearest TSS.
claims.source: Enhancers were located on average 77 kb from TSS, while promoters were located on average 106 kb from the nearest TSS, despite there being a greater number of peaks located <1 kb from the TSS (1008 enhancers vs. 9023 promoters; Figure 1B).
claims.evidence: This is supported by the data presented in Figure 1B.

claims.claim: A large fraction (0.41) of promoters were located >3 kb from an annotated TSS.
claims.source: This was an unexpected finding as a large fraction (0.41) of promoters were located >3 kb from an annotated TSS (see Appendix).
claims.evidence: This is supported by the data analysis described in the Results and Appendix.

claims.claim: H3K4me3 activity at enhancers is well established.
claims.source: H3K4me3 activity at enhancers is well established (Koch and Andrau, 2011; Pekowska et al., 2011); however, compared to H3K4me3 activity at promoters, H3K4me3 levels at enhancers are low (Calo and Wysocka, 2013).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to Koch and Andrau, 2011 and Pekowska et al., 2011.

claims.claim: Compared to H3K4me3 activity at promoters, H3K4me3 levels at enhancers are low.
claims.source: H3K4me3 activity at enhancers is well established (Koch and Andrau, 2011; Pekowska et al., 2011); however, compared to H3K4me3 activity at promoters, H3K4me3 levels at enhancers are low (Calo and Wysocka, 2013).
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to Calo and Wysocka, 2013.

claims.claim: H3K4me3 levels at enhancers were nearly seven times lower than those observed at promoter regions.
claims.source: This is in line with our observations that H3K4me3 levels at enhancers were nearly seven times lower than those observed at promoter regions (see Appendix for details).
claims.evidence: This is supported by the data analysis described in the Results and Appendix.

claims.claim: 12,295 high-confidence promoters were identified after grouping and filtering.
claims.source: Distance from TSS is frequently used to filter putative promoters from other elements, therefore, we grouped peaks characterized as promoters based on their distance to the nearest TSS (see Methods), resulting in 12,295 high-confidence promoters for all of the following analyses (see Appendix).
claims.evidence: This is supported by the data analysis described in the Results and Methods.

claims.claim: 35,677 putative enhancers and 8589 promoters were near genes with a one-to-one ortholog in mouse.
claims.source: To make use of resources available in model organisms such as GO databases, we converted all dunnart gene IDs to mouse orthologous genes for downstream applications. This reduced the dataset to 35,677 putative enhancers and 8589 promoters near (within 1 Mbp) genes with a one-to-one ortholog in mouse (Supplementary file 1a).
claims.evidence: This is supported by the data analysis described in the Results.

claims.claim: Gene annotations for both promoters and enhancers were enriched for 23% of the same GO terms.
claims.source: We found that gene annotations for both promoters and enhancers were enriched for 23% of the same GO terms, including cellular processes (protein localization to plasma membrane, protein localization to cell periphery, regulation of cell morphogenesis, positive regulation of cell migration) and development (axon development, camera-type eye development, muscle tissue development, striated muscle development).
claims.evidence: This is supported by the GO enrichment analysis described in the Results.

claims.claim: 44% of GO terms were uniquely enriched among genes assigned to promoters and were related to mRNA processing, transcription, mRNA stability, cell cycle, and mRNA degradation.
claims.source: By contrast, 44% of GO terms were uniquely enriched among genes assigned to promoters and were related to mRNA processing, transcription, mRNA stability, cell cycle, and mRNA degradation (Figure 2A, Supplementary file 1b) and uniquely enriched GO terms for genes assigned to candidate enhancers corresponded to processes indicative of early embryonic development (Figure 2A, Supplementary file 1c).
claims.evidence: This is supported by the GO enrichment analysis and data presented in Figure 2A.

claims.claim: Uniquely enriched GO terms for genes assigned to candidate enhancers corresponded to processes indicative of early embryonic development.
claims.source: By contrast, 44% of GO terms were uniquely enriched among genes assigned to promoters and were related to mRNA processing, transcription, mRNA stability, cell cycle, and mRNA degradation (Figure 2A, Supplementary file 1b) and uniquely enriched GO terms for genes assigned to candidate enhancers corresponded to processes indicative of early embryonic development (Figure 2A, Supplementary file 1c).
claims.evidence: This is supported by the GO enrichment analysis and data presented in Figure 2A.

claims.claim: Terms related to facial skeleton development were enriched among genes assigned to putative dunnart enhancers.
claims.source: Terms related to facial skeleton development were enriched among genes assigned to putative dunnart enhancers, including bone cell development, muscle cell development, secondary palate development, roof of mouth development, and mesenchyme development, consistent with dunnart craniofacial morphology (Cook et al., 2021).
claims.evidence: This is supported by the GO enrichment analysis and citation to Cook et al., 2021.

claims.claim: Enhancers active near important palate genes in the dunnart at birth may highlight potential regulatory mechanisms driving early palatal closure.
claims.source: Enhancers active near important palate genes (Won et al., 2023; Zarate et al., 2024) such as SHH, SATB2, MEF2C, SNAI2, and IRF6 in the dunnart at birth may highlight potential regulatory mechanisms driving early palatal closure.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the presence of enhancers near palate genes and citations to Won et al., 2023 and Zarate et al., 2024.

claims.claim: Terms related to the development of the circulatory system were enriched among genes linked to predicted enhancer regions.
claims.source: In addition, terms related to the development of the circulatory system, including regulation of vasculature development, circulatory system process, and blood circulation were enriched among genes linked to predicted enhancer regions (e.g., ACE, PDGFB, GATA4, GATA6, VEGFA).
claims.evidence: This is supported by the GO enrichment analysis described in the Results.

claims.claim: The oral region of newborn dunnarts is highly vascularized, with blood vessels visible through their translucent skin at birth.
claims.source: This is consistent with observations that show the oral region of newborn dunnarts is highly vascularized, with blood vessels visible through their translucent skin at birth (Cook et al., 2021).
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to Cook et al., 2021.

claims.claim: Enhancers were significantly enriched for 170 TFs relative to a background set of random GC- and length-matched sequences.
claims.source: Enhancers were significantly enriched for 170 TFs relative to a background set of random GC- and length-matched sequences (FDR-corrected, p < 0.01), including those with known roles in differentiation of cranial neural crest cells (TWIST, HOXA2), skeletal morphogenesis (DLX5, CREB5, HOXA2), bone development (ATF3, RUNX), cranial nerve development (ATOH1), and/or facial mesenchyme development (LHX2, FOXP1, MAFB; Figure 2B, Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This is supported by the motif enrichment analysis and data presented in Figure 2B.

claims.claim: TFBS in promoter sequences were dominated by transcriptional initiation regulatory sequences, with significant enrichment for 13 TFs.
claims.source: Consistent with the GO enrichment, TFBS in promoter sequences were dominated by transcriptional initiation regulatory sequences, with significant enrichment for 13 TFs (FDR-corrected, p < 0.01) including RFX3, RFX2, NRF, NRF1, GRY, ZBTB33, RONIN, JUND, and GFX (Figure 2B, Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This is supported by the motif enrichment analysis and data presented in Figure 2B.

claims.claim: There were 12,153 genes reproducibly expressed at a level >1 TPM across three biological replicates in dunnart face tissue.
claims.source: There were 12,153 genes reproducibly expressed at a level >1 TPM across three biological replicates, with the majority of genes expressed (67%; 8158/12,153) associated with an active enhancer and/or promoter peak.
claims.evidence: This is supported by the RNA-seq data analysis described in the Results.

claims.claim: The majority of genes expressed (67%; 8158/12,153) were associated with an active enhancer and/or promoter peak.
claims.source: There were 12,153 genes reproducibly expressed at a level >1 TPM across three biological replicates, with the majority of genes expressed (67%; 8158/12,153) associated with an active enhancer and/or promoter peak.
claims.evidence: This is supported by the integration of ChIP-seq and RNA-seq data.

claims.claim: Most enhancers (78% of all enhancers) were linked to a reproducibly expressed gene in the dunnart.
claims.source: Most enhancers (78% of all enhancers, Supplementary file 1d) or promoters (87% of all promoters, Supplementary file 1e) were linked to a reproducibly expressed gene in the dunnart (Figure 3A).
claims.evidence: This is supported by the integration of ChIP-seq and RNA-seq data presented in Figure 3A.

claims.claim: Most promoters (87% of all promoters) were linked to a reproducibly expressed gene in the dunnart.
claims.source: Most enhancers (78% of all enhancers, Supplementary file 1d) or promoters (87% of all promoters, Supplementary file 1e) were linked to a reproducibly expressed gene in the dunnart (Figure 3A).
claims.evidence: This is supported by the integration of ChIP-seq and RNA-seq data presented in Figure 3A.

claims.claim: The majority of reproducibly expressed genes near a regulatory peak (61%) were associated with both an enhancer and promoter region.
claims.source: Additionally, the majority of reproducibly expressed genes near a regulatory peak (61%) were associated with both an enhancer and promoter region (Figure 3B), highlighting the correspondence in active regulatory elements and expressed genes at this time point in the dunnart face.
claims.evidence: This is supported by the data presented in Figure 3B.

claims.claim: Genes with a medium-to-high expression level (>10 TPM) and associated with at least one putative enhancer and promoter were enriched for biological processes including 'in utero embryonic development', 'skeletal system development', 'muscle tissue development', 'skin development', 'vasculature development', and 'sensory organ development'.
claims.source: Genes with a medium-to-high expression level at this stage (>10 TPM) and associated with at least one putative enhancer and promoter were enriched for biological processes including 'in utero embryonic development', 'skeletal system development', 'muscle tissue development', 'skin development', 'vasculature development', and 'sensory organ development' (Figure 3C, Supplementary file 1f).
claims.evidence: This is supported by the GO enrichment analysis and data presented in Figure 3C.

claims.claim: Enrichment for the term 'in utero embryonic development' is indicative of the altricial nature of the dunnart neonate.
claims.source: Enrichment for the term 'in utero embryonic development' is indicative of the altricial nature of the dunnart neonate.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the GO enrichment results and knowledge of dunnart development.

claims.claim: In the dunnart, ossification begins post-birth (day of birth young corresponding approximately to embryonic day (E) 12.5 in mouse).
claims.source: In a previous study, we showed that in the dunnart, ossification begins post-birth (day of birth young corresponding approximately to embryonic day (E) 12.5 in mouse) and that the dunnart neonate instead likely relies on the well-developed cranial muscles and an extremely large chondrocranium for structural head and feeding support during early pouch life (Cook et al., 2021; Clark and Smith, 1993).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to Cook et al., 2021 and Clark and Smith, 1993.

claims.claim: The dunnart neonate likely relies on the well-developed cranial muscles and an extremely large chondrocranium for structural head and feeding support during early pouch life.
claims.source: In a previous study, we showed that in the dunnart, ossification begins post-birth (day of birth young corresponding approximately to embryonic day (E) 12.5 in mouse) and that the dunnart neonate instead likely relies on the well-developed cranial muscles and an extremely large chondrocranium for structural head and feeding support during early pouch life (Cook et al., 2021; Clark and Smith, 1993).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to Cook et al., 2021 and Clark and Smith, 1993.

claims.claim: High expression (>20 TPM) of key head myogenesis genes was observed in the dunnart.
claims.source: Consistent with this, we observed high expression (>20 TPM) of the key head myogenesis genes (Bentzinger et al., 2012; Buckingham, 2017; Lin et al., 2006), MYOD1, MYF6, MEF2C, PAX3, MYL1, and MYOG, essential genes regulating chondrogenesis (Lefebvre et al., 2019; Yip et al., 2019), SOX9, COL2A1, and FGFR1 and genes that act upstream of osteoblast differentiation (Qi et al., 2003; Huang et al., 2007), MSX1, MSX2, CEBPA/G, ALPL, DLX3, DLX5, FGFR1, and FGFR2 (Supplementary file 1d, e).
claims.evidence: This is supported by the RNA-seq data and citations to previous research.

claims.claim: Craniofacial development in the newborn dunnart is approximately equivalent to E12.5 in mouse.
claims.source: From our morphological study of dunnart craniofacial bone development, we estimated that craniofacial development in the newborn dunnart is approximately equivalent to E12.5 in mouse (Cook et al., 2021).
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to Cook et al., 2021.

claims.claim: ~17K enhancers and ~10K promoters per stage were found in the mouse after applying consistent peak calling and filtering parameters.
claims.source: After applying consistent peak calling and filtering parameters to the dunnart ChIP-seq data, we found ~17K enhancers and ~10K promoters per stage in the mouse (Figure 4A, see Appendix for details).
claims.evidence: This is supported by the analysis of mouse ENCODE data described in the Results.

claims.claim: The features of mouse predicted enhancer and promoters were consistent with the observations in the dunnart.
claims.source: The features of mouse predicted enhancer and promoters (percentage CpG, GC content, distance from TSS, peak length, and peak intensity) were consistent with the observations in the dunnart (Figure 4A, Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This is supported by the comparative analysis and data presented in Figure 4A and Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: The alignability (conserved sequence) for dunnart enhancers to the mouse genome was ~13% for 100 bp regions.
claims.source: The alignability (conserved sequence) for dunnart enhancers to the mouse genome was ~13% for 100 bp regions (Supplementary file 1v).
claims.evidence: This is supported by the whole-genome alignment analysis described in the Results.

claims.claim: Between 0.74% and 6.77% of enhancer regions out of all alignable enhancers were present in both mouse and dunnart.
claims.source: Between 0.74% and 6.77% of enhancer regions out of all alignable enhancers were present in both mouse and dunnart (Supplementary file 1g).
claims.evidence: This is supported by the comparative analysis of regulatory elements.

claims.claim: Between 45% and 57% of alignable promoter regions were present in mouse and dunnart.
claims.source: In contrast, between 45% and 57% of alignable promoter regions were present in mouse and dunnart (Supplementary file 1g).
claims.evidence: This is supported by the comparative analysis of regulatory elements.

claims.claim: Promoter regions are more stable over large evolutionary distances than enhancers.
claims.source: Although this is a small fraction of the total peaks (~8% for promoters and ~0.5% of enhancers; Supplementary file 1g), it suggests that, consistent with the literature (Villar et al., 2015), promoter regions are more stable over large evolutionary distances and that shifts in developmental timing of craniofacial marsupials may be more likely to be driven by recently evolved enhancer regions in marsupials.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the comparative data and citation to Villar et al., 2015.

claims.claim: Shifts in developmental timing of craniofacial marsupials may be more likely to be driven by recently evolved enhancer regions in marsupials.
claims.source: Although this is a small fraction of the total peaks (~8% for promoters and ~0.5% of enhancers; Supplementary file 1g), it suggests that, consistent with the literature (Villar et al., 2015), promoter regions are more stable over large evolutionary distances and that shifts in developmental timing of craniofacial marsupials may be more likely to be driven by recently evolved enhancer regions in marsupials.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the comparative data.

claims.claim: Regions with conserved activity between mouse and dunnart were predominantly near genes consistently expressed in both and were enriched for core craniofacial developmental and signaling processes.
claims.source: Despite this, regions with conserved activity between the two species were predominantly near genes consistently expressed in both and were enriched for core craniofacial developmental and signaling processes.
claims.evidence: This is supported by the comparative analysis of regulatory elements and gene expression.

claims.claim: Predicted dunnart enhancers with sequence conservation in mouse and matching peak activity at any of the five mouse embryonic stages (461 regions) were located near genes reproducibly expressed (>1 TPM, 89%) in both species.
claims.source: Predicted dunnart enhancers with sequence conservation in mouse and matching peak activity at any of the five mouse embryonic stages (461 regions) were located near genes reproducibly expressed (>1 TPM, 89%) in both species (Supplementary file 1h).
claims.evidence: This is supported by the comparative analysis of regulatory elements and gene expression.

claims.claim: Genes near conserved enhancers were enriched for core developmental and signaling processes: BMP signaling, cartilage development, ossification, skeletal development, and chondrocyte differentiation.
claims.source: Genes in this group were enriched for core developmental and signaling processes: BMP signaling, cartilage development, ossification, skeletal development, and chondrocyte differentiation (Supplementary file 1i).
claims.evidence: This is supported by the GO enrichment analysis of genes near conserved enhancers.

claims.claim: For the 4311 dunnart-specific enhancers, 2310 (54%) were linked to genes expressed >1 TPM in all stages and species.
claims.source: Taking the predicted dunnart enhancers alignable to the mouse but without a matching peak, we looked at nearby genes and compared expression between mouse and dunnart. For the 4311 dunnart-specific enhancers, we found that 2310 (54%) were linked to genes expressed >1 TPM in all stages and species, suggesting that these genes in mouse could be regulated by a different set of regulatory regions or could be accounted for by the reduced enrichment in the mouse ENCODE ChIP-seq face datasets for H3K27ac (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).

results.result: The authors identified 60,626 putative enhancers and 12,295 high-confidence promoters in dunnart craniofacial tissue using ChIP-seq for H3K27ac and H3K4me3 marks. This represents the first genome-wide characterization of face regulatory elements in a marsupial.
results.evaluation: Claims C5, C36, C37, C42, and C49 provide consistent quantitative data from ChIP-seq analysis showing identification of regulatory elements. The methodology is clearly described, quality controls were performed (immunofluorescence validation, qPCR), and filtering criteria are documented. Claim C6 regarding novelty is supported by the absence of prior similar studies in marsupials.

results.result: The distribution of histone marks in dunnart craniofacial tissue shows that 62% of H3K4me3 peaks co-occur with H3K27ac, while 50% of H3K27ac peaks are unique. H3K4me3 levels at enhancers are approximately seven times lower than at promoters, consistent with established patterns in other species.
results.evaluation: Claims C38-C48 describe the chromatin mark distribution patterns supported by ChIP-seq data (Figure 1A) and are consistent with cited literature (Villar et al., 2015; Cain et al., 2011; Santos-Rosa et al., 2002). The quantitative measurements and comparisons are clearly presented and align with expected biological patterns.

results.result: Enhancers were located on average 77 kb from TSS while promoters were on average 106 kb from TSS, with a large fraction (0.41) of promoters located >3 kb from annotated TSS.
results.evaluation: Claims C43-C45 present unexpected findings regarding promoter distances from TSS. While the data are presented (Figure 1B), the authors acknowledge this as unexpected and note that 41% of promoters are >3 kb from TSS, which is unusual. The authors address this through additional filtering to generate high-confidence promoters, but the biological interpretation remains unclear and may reflect annotation limitations.

results.result: GO enrichment analysis reveals that genes near enhancers are enriched for developmental processes including facial skeleton development, muscle development, and circulatory system development, while genes near promoters are enriched for mRNA processing and transcription. Motif analysis identified 170 enriched transcription factors in enhancers and 13 in promoters.
results.evaluation: Claims C51-C59 describe GO enrichment and motif analysis results supported by data in Figure 2A-B. The analyses use appropriate methods (clusterProfiler, HOMER) with proper statistical corrections (FDR < 0.01). The biological interpretations are consistent with known craniofacial development processes and are supported by citations to relevant literature.

results.result: RNA-seq analysis identified 12,153 genes reproducibly expressed in dunnart face tissue, with 67% associated with active regulatory elements. The majority of enhancers (78%) and promoters (87%) are linked to expressed genes, and highly expressed genes (>10 TPM) with both enhancer and promoter activity are enriched for developmental processes.
results.evaluation: Claims C60-C65 integrate ChIP-seq and RNA-seq data showing correspondence between regulatory elements and gene expression (Figure 3A-C). The quantitative measurements are clearly presented, biological replicates are used (n=3), and the GO enrichment analysis is appropriately conducted. The high concordance between regulatory marks and expression supports the functional relevance of identified elements.

results.result: The dunnart neonate at birth corresponds developmentally to approximately E12.5 in mouse, with ossification beginning post-birth. High expression of key myogenesis, chondrogenesis, and osteoblast differentiation genes supports reliance on cranial muscles and chondrocranium for structural support.
results.evaluation: Claims C67-C70 are supported by RNA-seq data showing high expression (>20 TPM) of relevant developmental genes and citations to previous morphological studies (Cook et al., 2021; Clark and Smith, 1993). The developmental staging comparison to mouse is based on prior morphological work and is consistent with the gene expression patterns observed.

results.result: Comparative analysis with mouse ENCODE data reveals that only ~0.5% of enhancers and ~8% of promoters show sequence conservation and matching activity between dunnart and mouse. Promoters are more stable over evolutionary distances than enhancers, suggesting that developmental timing shifts may be driven by species-specific enhancers.
results.evaluation: Claims C71-C77 present comparative genomic analysis using whole-genome alignments and consistent peak-calling methods. The low conservation rates are expected given the ~170 million year divergence and are supported by citations to literature on sequence turnover (Villar et al., 2015; Genereux et al., 2020). The inference about enhancer-driven heterochrony (C77) is reasonable but remains speculative.

results.result: Conserved regulatory elements between mouse and dunnart (461 enhancers) are predominantly near genes expressed in both species and enriched for core craniofacial developmental processes including BMP signaling, cartilage development, and skeletal development.
results.evaluation: Claims C78-C80 describe analysis of conserved regulatory elements with matching activity. The integration of sequence conservation, ChIP-seq peaks, and gene expression data is methodologically sound. The GO enrichment for core developmental processes is well-supported and biologically meaningful, indicating conservation of fundamental craniofacial regulatory networks.

results.result: A subset of 179 dunnart-specific enhancers (114 unique genes) are near genes highly expressed only in dunnart, including genes involved in cranial neural crest proliferation, embryonic myogenesis, keratinocyte proliferation, and sensory system development.
results.evaluation: Claims C81-C83 and C9 identify dunnart-specific regulatory elements through comparative analysis of ChIP-seq and RNA-seq data. The filtering criteria (>10 TPM in dunnart, low/no expression in mouse E10.5-E15.5) are clearly defined. The biological interpretation is supported by the specific genes identified and their known functions in relevant developmental processes.

results.result: Gene-level comparison reveals that 56% of genes near enhancers are unique to dunnart. Genes highly expressed in dunnart but not mouse (537 genes) are enriched for three main processes: epidermis/skin development, sensory system development, and muscle development, with 'sensory system development' being uniquely enriched in dunnart.
results.evaluation: Claims C84-C87 and C10 present gene-level comparative analysis supported by data in Figure 5A-D. The identification of dunnart-specific expression patterns uses appropriate thresholds and GO enrichment analysis. The finding of sensory system enrichment is particularly well-supported and biologically relevant to marsupial life history.

results.result: Genes critical for keratinocyte development and mechanosensory system development, including KRT17, KRT8, and ATOH1, are highly expressed in dunnart facial tissue compared to mouse. These genes are essential for establishing innervation patterns and Merkel cell specification.
results.evaluation: Claims C88-C92 are supported by RNA-seq data (Figure 5D-E) showing differential expression of keratin genes and mechanosensory genes. The biological interpretation is strengthened by citations to functional studies (Doucet et al., 2013; Xiao et al., 2014) demonstrating the roles of these genes in sensory development. The comparative expression patterns are clearly documented.

results.result: High expression of olfactory system genes (CCK, OTX1, ISLR, YBX3) and muscle contraction genes (TNNI2, TNNT3, CAR3, ATP2A2, IGFBP6, TRIM72) was observed in dunnart craniofacial tissue.
results.evaluation: Claims C93-C94 are supported by RNA-seq data and citations to literature establishing the functions of these genes. The expression patterns are consistent with the accelerated development of sensory and muscular systems in marsupials. The data presentation in Figure 5D and supplementary files provides clear evidence.

results.result: The majority of conserved toolkit genes involved in embryonic development show consistent expression between mouse and dunnart, with significant overlap in genes near regulatory elements and high concordance in enriched biological processes, supporting the importance of conserved genes and pathways in mammalian facial development.
results.evaluation: Claims C95, C7, C108, and C109 describe conservation of core developmental genes and pathways. This is supported by comparative gene expression analysis (Figure 5—figure supplement 2) and gene-level comparisons showing substantial overlap despite low sequence conservation. The conclusion is strengthened by citation to Roosenboom et al., 2016 and is biologically reasonable.

results.result: Temporal clustering analysis reveals that dunnart-expressed genes associate with two mouse gene clusters: one upregulated at E15.5 (cluster 2, OR=1.30) enriched for sensory perception and skin development, and one upregulated at E14.5 (cluster 3, OR=1.99) enriched for muscle development, suggesting shifts in developmental timing of these systems.
results.evaluation: Claims C96-C100 present temporal clustering analysis using appropriate methods (TCseq, fuzzy c-means clustering). The statistical analysis includes odds ratios with confidence intervals, and the cluster validation uses the Calinski criterion. The biological interpretation linking temporal shifts to marsupial life history is well-reasoned and supported by the enrichment patterns (Figure 6A-D).

results.result: Dunnarts exhibit high expression of periderm-related genes including KRT17 and retain the periderm post-birth, unlike placental mammals. This retention may relate to neonatal transcutaneous gas exchange, with lung respiration beginning around 5 days postpartum coinciding with periderm disappearance.
results.evaluation: Claims C113-C117 are supported by gene expression data and multiple citations to literature on marsupial periderm biology (Smith and Keyte, 2020; Simpson et al., 2011; Hammond et al., 2019). The connection between periderm retention and gas exchange is well-established in the cited literature, and the gene expression patterns are consistent with this biology.

results.result: Newborn marsupials require highly developed mechanosensory and olfactory systems for the journey to the pouch. The snout epidermis shows mature Merkel cells at birth, while in mouse Merkel cell development begins at E16.5. Upregulation of Merkel cell genes in dunnart likely reflects prioritization of sensory development for ex utero survival.
results.evaluation: Claims C118-C121 and C11 integrate gene expression data with established marsupial biology from multiple cited studies (Veitch et al., 2000; Jones and Munger, 1985; Jenkins et al., 2019). The inference about prioritization of sensory development (C121, C11) is well-reasoned given the biological context and gene expression patterns, though it remains somewhat speculative.

results.result: In marsupials, pharyngeal muscles are well differentiated before birth and undergo considerable differentiation in the first 2 days after birth, preceding development of the central nervous system and skeletal system. This pattern differs from rodents where skeletal and muscular development occur simultaneously.
results.evaluation: Claims C110-C112 are supported by citations to Smith, 1994, which provides comparative developmental data. These claims establish important biological context for interpreting the gene expression results but represent prior knowledge rather than new findings from this study.

results.result: The regulatory landscape varies significantly between mouse and dunnart, and accelerated face development in the dunnart may be driven by dunnart-specific enhancer activity. Craniofacial developmental constraints may be driven by dunnart-specific gene regulation.
results.evaluation: Claims C8, C12, C77, and C122 represent the main conclusions integrating all results. The variation in regulatory landscape (C8) is well-documented through comparative ChIP-seq analysis. The inferences about enhancer-driven heterochrony (C12, C77, C122) are reasonable given the data showing species-specific enhancers near developmentally relevant genes, though causality is not directly demonstrated.

results.result: A de novo dunnart genome assembly was generated with total size 2.84 Gb, N50 of 23 Mb, BUSCO completeness of 89.9%, and GC content of ~36.25%, comparable to other marsupial genomes.
results.evaluation: Claims C123-C126 describe the genome assembly with standard quality metrics. The BUSCO score of 89.9% and N50 of 23 Mb indicate reasonable quality for downstream analyses. Comparison to other marsupial genomes (C125, C126) is supported by citations and shows the assembly is of comparable quality, though not exceptional by current standards.

results.result: Marsupials and placentals exhibit fundamental differences in reproductive strategies and craniofacial development. Marsupials show accelerated orofacial development including nasal cavity, tongue, bones, musculature, and peripheral nervous system, with less interspecies variation than placentals. The molecular mechanisms underlying these differences remain poorly understood, and the dunnart provides an ideal model for comparative studies.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C35 and C101-C105 establish biological background and rationale for the study. These are well-supported by extensive citations to established literature on marsupial and placental development. The claims about the dunnart as a model system (C32-C35) are supported by citations to recent work. These provide essential context but represent prior knowledge rather than new findings.

results.result: After converting dunnart gene IDs to mouse orthologs, 35,677 putative enhancers and 8589 promoters were near genes with one-to-one orthologs in mouse.
results.evaluation: Claim C50 describes a necessary data processing step for comparative analysis. The conversion through Tasmanian devil to mouse orthologs is clearly described and appropriate given the lack of direct dunnart GO annotations. The reduction in dataset size is expected and documented.

results.result: Regulatory elements in the dunnart were largely not sequence conserved in the mouse (~8% for promoters and ~0.5% of enhancers) given the large evolutionary distance (~170 million years) and high turnover of non-coding DNA sequences.
results.evaluation: Claim C106 summarizes the low sequence conservation finding, which is well-supported by the whole-genome alignment analysis and consistent with cited literature on non-coding sequence evolution (Genereux et al., 2020; Andrews et al., 2023). The evolutionary distance context is appropriate.

results.result: The authors assembled a new dunnart genome with total size of 2.84 Gb, N50 of 23 Mb, BUSCO completeness of 89.9%, and G+C content of ~36.25%, which is comparable to other marsupial genomes.
results.evaluation: Reviewers explicitly praised the genome assembly, stating 'The genome assembly method was thorough, using two different long-read methods (Pacbio and ONT)' and noting it 'will benefit many future studies.' The editor called it 'compelling data, including a new dunnart genome assembly.'

results.result: This is the first genome-wide description of face regulatory elements in a marsupial, identifying 60,626 putative enhancers and 12,295 high-confidence promoters through ChIP-seq analysis of H3K4me3 and H3K27ac marks in dunnart craniofacial tissue.
results.evaluation: Reviewers affirmed this is 'one of the few epigenomic studies performed in marsupials (of any organ) and the first performed in fat-tailed dunnart' and praised it as addressing 'the lack of knowledge' about regulatory profiles in marsupial craniofacial development. The editor described the data as 'compelling.'

results.result: Genes near dunnart enhancers and promoters were enriched for biological processes related to craniofacial development including skeletal development, muscle development, skin development, vasculature development, and sensory organ development, with 67% of expressed genes associated with active regulatory elements.
results.evaluation: Reviewers stated that the authors 'found that genes proximal to these regulatory loci were enriched for functions related to bone, skin, muscle and embryonic development, verifying the precocious state of newborn dunnart facial tissue.' This finding was accepted without critique.

results.result: While genes involved in facial development were largely conserved between mouse and dunnart, the regulatory landscape varied significantly, with only ~0.5% of enhancers but ~8% of promoters showing sequence conservation, suggesting promoters are more stable over evolutionary distances and that developmental timing shifts may be driven by recently evolved enhancer regions.
results.evaluation: Reviewers noted 'the authors found a much higher proportion of promoter regions aligned between species than for enhancer regions' and that 'subsequent profiling identified regulatory elements conserved across species.' They also stated the study 'provides evidence supporting the important role enhancer elements play in mammalian phenotypic evolution, relative to promoters.'

results.result: A subset of 179 dunnart-specific enhancers were associated with genes highly expressed only in dunnart (>10 TPM) relating to cranial neural crest proliferation, embryonic myogenesis, epidermis development, and sensory system development, suggesting accelerated face development may be driven by dunnart-specific enhancer activity.
results.evaluation: Reviewers affirmed that 'identification of dunnart-specific enhancers and patterns of RNA expression further confirm the precocious state of muscle development, as well as for sensory system development, in dunnart.' The editor noted that 'enhancer regulatory elements as primary driver of this difference' was a key finding.

results.result: Comparative RNA-seq revealed dunnart-specific expression of genes involved in mechanosensory system development (including KRT17, KRT8, ATOH1), olfactory system development, and muscle development, with temporal clustering showing dunnart genes associated with mouse E14.5-E15.5 expression patterns despite morphological similarity to E12.5, suggesting shifts in developmental timing of skin, muscle, and sensory perception.
results.evaluation: Reviewers stated the findings 'confirm the precocious state of muscle development, as well as for sensory system development, in dunnart, suggesting that early formation of these features are critical for neonate marsupials.' The editor described the study as showing 'marsupial craniofacial tissue develops in a precocious manner.'

results.result: Accelerated development of the dunnart sensory system, including upregulation of Merkel cell genes, likely relates to sensory cues received during the postnatal journey to the pouch, as newborn marsupials require highly developed mechanosensory and olfactory systems for survival.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accepted this interpretation, noting the study helps 'elucidate the regulatory profile underlying craniofacial heterochrony' and that findings relate to 'the advanced craniofacial development required for joey survival.' No concerns were raised about this inference.

results.result: Newborn dunnarts exhibit high expression of KRT17 and other periderm-related genes, and unlike placental mammals, marsupials retain the periderm post-birth, which may relate to neonatal transcutaneous gas exchange observed in the first few days after birth.
results.evaluation: This finding is part of the broader pattern of dunnart-specific gene expression that reviewers praised. They noted the study confirms 'the precocious state' of various developmental systems including skin development, and raised no concerns about these specific claims.

results.result: In dunnart, ossification begins post-birth (corresponding to approximately E12.5 in mouse), with high expression of myogenesis, chondrogenesis, and osteoblast differentiation genes, and the neonate likely relies on well-developed cranial muscles and large chondrocranium for structural support, contrasting with simultaneous skeletal and muscular development in rodents.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accepted the developmental staging and comparative analysis, noting 'previous work from the authors have shown that the younger mouse samples (E11.5-12.5) approximately corresponds to the dunnart developmental stage.' The findings about muscle and skeletal development were part of the accepted 'precocious state' characterization.

results.result: Analysis of mouse ENCODE data using consistent parameters identified ~17K enhancers and ~10K promoters per stage, with features (CpG content, GC content, distance from TSS, peak length, intensity) consistent with dunnart observations.
results.evaluation: While reviewers praised the comparative approach and noted 'the authors found a much higher proportion of promoter regions aligned between species,' they also identified a key weakness: data from 'a single developmental time point of the fat-tailed dunnart' compared to 'six developmental time points' in mouse. The reviewer suggested 'it would be useful to have samples from at least one older dunnart time point' to better assess developmental dynamics.

results.result: Background context establishing that marsupials and placentals differ in reproductive strategies, with marsupials showing accelerated orofacial development, less morphological variation, and that the fat-tailed dunnart is an emerging model species with one of the shortest gestations, while molecular mechanisms underlying these differences remain poorly understood.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accepted this background context, noting 'The birth of altricial young in marsupials is an important feature of their development that is distinct from placental mammals' and that 'Very little is known, however, about the regulatory profile that contributes to the advanced craniofacial development.' These claims provide accepted context for the study.

results.result: Technical and methodological findings including histone mark characteristics, distance distributions of regulatory elements from TSS, ortholog mapping, specific gene associations, and the overall conclusion that craniofacial developmental constraints may be driven by dunnart-specific gene regulation.
results.evaluation: Reviewers praised the 'thorough analysis' and noted the genome was 'effectively annotated and used for functional analysis of orthologous regulatory elements.' The overall conclusion about dunnart-specific regulation driving developmental constraints aligns with the reviewers' summary that the study shows 'enhancer regulatory elements as primary driver of this difference.'

comparisons.comparison: Perfect agreement on genome assembly quality (C123-C126). Both evaluations praise the assembly methods and quality metrics, with reviewers explicitly noting it was 'thorough' and 'will benefit many future studies.'

Perfect agreement on background context (C1-C35, C101-C105). Both accept the established literature on marsupial development and the rationale for studying dunnart craniofacial development. These claims provide foundational context rather than new findings.

Strong agreement on ChIP-seq methodology and novelty (C5, C6, C36, C37, C42, C49). OpenEval emphasizes quality controls and methodology; peer reviewers praise this as 'one of the few epigenomic studies in marsupials' with 'compelling data.' Peer review also includes chromatin mark claims (C38, C39) not in OpenEval R1.

Partial overlap on chromatin mark distribution (C38, C39). OpenEval R2 covers C38-C41, C46-C48 describing chromatin patterns; peer R2 only mentions C38-C39 alongside the novelty claims. Both find the data compelling.

Strong agreement on GO enrichment and motif analysis (C51-C59). OpenEval emphasizes methodological rigor; peer reviewers accept findings that genes near regulatory elements are 'enriched for functions related to bone, skin, muscle and embryonic development.' Peer R3 also includes RNA-seq integration claims (C60-C65).

Agreement on ChIP-seq and RNA-seq integration (C60-C65). OpenEval highlights concordance between regulatory marks and expression; peer reviewers accept this as verifying 'the precocious state of newborn dunnart facial tissue.'

Agreement on developmental staging and gene expression (C67-C70). OpenEval supports claims based on RNA-seq data and morphological comparisons; peer reviewers accept the staging, noting 'previous work from the authors have shown' the mouse-dunnart correspondence. Peer R9 also includes broader developmental context (C110-C112).
Agreement on comparative developmental context (C110-C112). Both evaluations accept these claims from Smith, 1994 as established background knowledge supporting the study's comparative framework.

Divergent evaluations on comparative genomic analysis (C71-C77). OpenEval finds low conservation rates expected and well-supported; peer reviewers raise concerns about comparing 'a single developmental time point' in dunnart to 'six developmental time points' in mouse, suggesting additional time points would strengthen claims.

Partial agreement on sequence conservation patterns (C73-C76). OpenEval R7 addresses low enhancer conservation; peer R4 accepts that 'a much higher proportion of promoter regions aligned between species than for enhancer regions,' supporting the evolutionary interpretation.

Agreement on conserved regulatory elements (C78-C80). OpenEval emphasizes methodological soundness of integrating conservation with activity; peer reviewers note 'subsequent profiling identified regulatory elements conserved across species' and accept the finding.

Agreement on conservation of core developmental pathways (C7, C95, C108, C109). Both evaluations accept that despite low sequence conservation, core developmental genes and pathways are conserved. Peer reviewers note this 'provides evidence supporting the important role enhancer elements play in mammalian phenotypic evolution.'

Agreement on low sequence conservation finding (C106). Both accept this as well-supported by whole-genome alignment analysis and consistent with evolutionary distance between marsupials and placentals.

Agreement on dunnart-specific regulatory elements (C9, C81-C83). OpenEval emphasizes clear filtering criteria; peer reviewers affirm 'identification of dunnart-specific enhancers' confirms precocious development. Peer R5 also includes the heterochrony inference (C12, C77).

Agreement on enhancer-driven heterochrony conclusions (C8, C12, C77, C122). OpenEval notes these inferences are reasonable though causality not directly demonstrated; peer reviewers accept 'enhancer regulatory elements as primary driver of this difference' as a key finding.

Agreement on dunnart-specific gene expression patterns (C10, C87). OpenEval emphasizes sensory system enrichment; peer reviewers accept findings 'confirm the precocious state of muscle development, as well as for sensory system development.' Peer R6 covers broader set including temporal clustering (C88-C93, C96-C100).

Agreement on keratin and mechanosensory gene expression (C88-C92). OpenEval highlights RNA-seq data and functional citations; peer reviewers accept these as confirming 'the precocious state' critical for neonate marsupials.
Agreement on muscle and sensory gene expression (C93-C94). Both evaluations accept these findings as supporting accelerated development of systems needed for joey survival.

Agreement on temporal clustering analysis (C96-C100). OpenEval emphasizes methodological rigor of clustering and statistical validation; peer reviewers accept the temporal shifts as part of the broader pattern confirming precocious development.

Perfect agreement on periderm biology findings (C113-C117). OpenEval cites established marsupial periderm literature; peer reviewers accept these as part of the dunnart-specific gene expression patterns without raising concerns.

Agreement on sensory development prioritization (C11, C118-C121). OpenEval notes the inference is well-reasoned but somewhat speculative; peer reviewers accept the interpretation that findings relate to 'the advanced craniofacial development required for joey survival.'

OpenEval flags unexpected promoter-TSS distances (C43-C45) as UNCERTAIN due to unusual findings and potential annotation limitations. Peer review R12 does not specifically address these claims, grouping them with other methodological details as part of 'thorough analysis.'

Both accept the GO annotation conversion methodology (C50). OpenEval describes it as necessary and appropriate; peer reviewers praise the genome as 'effectively annotated and used for functional analysis.'

Agreement on variation in regulatory landscape (C8). Both evaluations accept this as a main conclusion well-documented through comparative ChIP-seq analysis, with peer reviewers emphasizing the role of enhancers in phenotypic evolution.
